record.file_problem: Text appears complete; referenced plots are not included in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies weak-to-strong fine-tuning and evaluates the result with PGR, using new models and NLP datasets.
record.gate_note: The post reports the basic PGR result in aggregate across datasets. It also reports qualitative outcomes for other interventions. Probe-based results are not separately rowed because the supplied text gives no separate explicit outcomes for the named claim versions; the referenced plots are unavailable.
record.test_reason: Reruns the Burns et al. setup (weak soft labels, strong student, ground-truth ceiling, PGR) with Qwen1.5 0.5B supervising Llama3 8B on 25 NLP datasets. It reports PGR > 0 and tests several training changes against the default.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find basic weak-to-strong generalization consistently across NLP tasks, but none of their interventions consistently improves it. Only log-confidence loss shows possible weak signs of helping. They suggest vanilla weak-to-strong training may already elicit most of what the strong model knows. They caution that their negative results may not hold for larger models, and that weak-to-strong generalization needs ground-truth validation and is not a complete solution to scalable oversight.
record.recipe_differences: Retains weak-supervisor labels, strong-student fine-tuning, and ROC AUC/PGR evaluation, but tests Llama3 8B with Qwen1.5 0.5B on open-source NLP datasets using LoRA; the default setup includes auxiliary log-confidence loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary across datasets. Log-confidence loss is better than cross-entropy on 16 of 21 datasets, but the aggregate statistical evidence is weak.

fits_no_version.finding: Probes on Llama3 8B activations (kNN, logistic regression) do best at middle layers (layer 16 of 32), kNN k≈50 and L2 penalty 1e-2. This is measured as probe ROC AUC minus weak-label ROC AUC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear or kNN probes on a strong model's middle-layer activations, fit to weak labels, can exceed the weak labels' accuracy, with performance depending on layer and regularization.

record.problems: Only one weak/strong model-size pairing is tested. Most outcome comparisons are qualitative or aggregate, per-dataset PGR values are not given in the text, and the referenced plots are unavailable in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Probe prediction, filtering, and relabelling experiments are described as performing poorly relative to vanilla weak-to-strong training, but the supplied text gives no separate explicit outcome values for those experiments. No rows were left out among the directly reported PGR and loss-comparison results.

untested.parts: Only one supervisor/student pairing (0.5B to 8B). The text gives no per-dataset PGR magnitudes.
Ensembling weak supervisors. Larger scales, where Burns et al. find log-confidence more effective.
Variation with supervisor or student size. Chess and reward modelling. Which representations predict PGR. The text gives no quantified task dependence.
Not tested: exploitation of what the supervisor cannot check, distribution shift, shared errors.
No vision or other non-language modality.

missing.what: Probe-based interventions (probe predictions, filtering with kNN, logistic regression or TopoFilter, probe relabelling) all 'perform poorly compared to vanilla weak-to-strong training', with some extremely low PGRs. rows_left_out wrongly says the text gives no explicit outcome.

record.verdict_notes: This is a blog post and not peer reviewed; the plots are not in the text. The reader's V2 'supports' label for log-confidence is too strong given the non-significant tests and is replaced by limits_scope. The reader's V3 'supports' label is dropped because R7 cannot show task dependence of PGR.

versions.untested_parts: No broad model-size sweep; four saturated datasets do not permit a clear PGR assessment.
Ensembling weak supervisors is not tested. The text does not give numerical PGR values for the loss comparisons.
Only NLP datasets and one weak/strong size pairing are tested; no chess, reward-modelling, or size sweep. The text does not establish which representations predict PGR.
No reported test of supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, or shared errors.
No theory test or result about necessary conditions for beating a supervisor.
No vision or other non-language modality.
